claim: Olaus Magnus's Carta Marina, a large map of Scandinavia published in 1539, is famous for the sea monsters drawn in its waters.
fact_check_evidence: Smithsonian Magazine and the Biodiversity Heritage Library describe the sea monsters on Olaus Magnus's 1539 Carta Marina. (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/five-real-sea-monsters-brought-life-early-naturalists-180953155/ https://blog.biodiversitylibrary.org/2014/10/release-kraken)

claim: Kraken tales were likely fed by rotted remains of giant squid and large octopuses washing up on beaches, which people tried to explain.
fact_check_evidence: The Biodiversity Heritage Library and Smithsonian Magazine link the kraken legend to giant squid seen or stranded in northern seas. (https://blog.biodiversitylibrary.org/2014/10/release-kraken https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/five-real-sea-monsters-brought-life-early-naturalists-180953155/)

claim: Since 1986, over 19 million volunteers in Ocean Conservancy's International Coastal Cleanup have collected over 400 million pounds (about 181 million kg) of trash.
fact_check_evidence: Ocean Conservancy's 2025 advisory and Save The Bay report similar totals (nearly 20 million volunteers, over 405 million pounds since 1986). (https://oceanconservancy.org/newsroom/press-release/2025/09/03/advisory-worlds-largest-beach-cleanup-celebrates-40th-year-in-september/ https://savebay.org/ocean-conservancys-annual-report-highlights-the-global-impact-of-local-volunteers-cleaning-up-local-waterways/)

claim: Cleanup volunteers record every item they collect by type, and the tallies show which items to target and whether rules work.
fact_check_evidence: Ocean Conservancy's cleanup reports and Save The Bay describe item-by-item data used to inform policy. (https://savebay.org/ocean-conservancys-annual-report-highlights-the-global-impact-of-local-volunteers-cleaning-up-local-waterways/ https://www.surfer.com/news/ocean-conservancy-icc-plastic-bottles-2025)
